trail.title: The California Mission Trail
trail.start_point: Mission San Diego de Alcala, San Diego
trail.best_season: Year-round; spring and fall are mildest
trail.summary_short: Twenty-one Spanish missions founded between 1769 and 1823, strung a day's travel apart along El Camino Real from San Diego to Sonoma. Most are still working Catholic churches, and each one has its own page here.
trail.the_story:
In 1769 Spain moved north from Baja California to hold Alta California, and the Franciscans went with the soldiers. Over the next fifty-four years they founded twenty-one missions between San Diego and Sonoma, each roughly a day's travel from the next -- about thirty miles -- strung along the road that came to be called El Camino Real, the Royal Road. Nine are credited to St. Junipero Serra, nine to his successor Fr. Fermin Francisco de Lasuen, and the last three to Frs. Estevan Tapis, Vicente Francisco de Sarria, and Jose Altimira.

The missions were farms, workshops, and churches at once. They introduced wheat, cattle, olives, and wine to California, and the pueblos that grew up beside them became Los Angeles, San Francisco, San Jose, and Santa Cruz. They were also built by Native Californians -- Kumeyaay, Tongva, Chumash, Salinan, Esselen, Ohlone, Yokuts, Luiseno, Tataviam, Coast Miwok, Pomo, Wappo, Patwin and others -- who lived under Franciscan control, and whose descendants are still here.

After Mexican independence the missions were secularized in the 1830s and most fell into ruin. Some were returned to the Church by the United States government in the 1860s; others were rebuilt over the following century. Today most are working parishes, four are minor basilicas, three are state historic parks, and one is a university chapel. The chain is marked along U.S. 101 and older highway alignments by cast-iron mission bells hung on shepherd's-crook posts, the first of them placed in 1906.
trail.church_recognition:
The missions are Catholic places, and their history is not a simple one. The California Missions Foundation, which stewards the chain, states plainly that mission life was "highly coercive" and "controlled by the padres," that baptized people "were not allowed to leave without permission," that "corporal punishment, such as floggings, for Native Americans who disobeyed the rules was frequent and at times severe," that missionaries "discouraged aspects of Native religion and culture," and that "disease frequently ravaged mission communities." Native peoples resisted: at San Diego in 1775, at Mission San Jose in 1828 under Estanislao, and in the Chumash uprising of 1824 that began at Santa Ines.

The Church has acknowledged this directly. Speaking in Bolivia on July 9, 2015, Pope Francis said: "I humbly ask forgiveness, not only for the offenses of the Church herself, but also for crimes committed against the native peoples during the so-called conquest of America." Archbishop Jose Gomez of Los Angeles has written that "the exploitation of America's first peoples, the destruction of their ancient civilizations, is a historic tragedy," that "crimes committed against their ancestors continue to shape the lives and futures of native peoples today," and that "it is sadly true that corporal punishment was sometimes used in the missions."

St. Junipero Serra was canonized by Pope Francis in Washington, D.C., on September 23, 2015. The canonization remains contested, and Catholics of good faith disagree about it. A pilgrim can hold both truths at once: that these are consecrated places where the Eucharist has been offered for two and a half centuries, and that they were built at a cost borne by people who did not choose it. Many of their descendants are Catholic today, and several missions are their parishes.
trail.catholic_teaching:
A mission church teaches the same thing every parish church teaches: that God chose to meet people in a particular place, through the sacraments, in the company of a community. What makes the chain worth walking as a whole is what it says about time. These twenty-one churches have kept the same Mass through Spanish rule, Mexican rule, secularization, ruin, earthquake, fire, and restoration.

The missions also ask something harder of the Church: to tell the truth about its own past. The Catechism teaches that the Church is holy and always in need of purification, and that repentance is not weakness but honesty. A pilgrimage along El Camino Real that skips that part is not a pilgrimage; it is a sightseeing tour.
trail.walking_the_route:
This is a driving route, not a walking one. The full chain runs about 600 miles from San Diego north to Sonoma, largely along U.S. 101 and older highway alignments, and most pilgrims take one to two weeks to do all twenty-one, or a long weekend for a region. Southern California (San Diego to San Fernando), the Central Coast (San Buenaventura to Carmel), and the Bay Area and north (Santa Clara to Sonoma) each make a natural leg.

The missions are not all the same kind of place. Most are active parishes with daily or Sunday Mass; La Purisima, Santa Cruz, and San Francisco Solano are California state historic parks with admission fees and park hours; Santa Clara is a university chapel on the Santa Clara University campus; San Antonio de Padua sits inside Fort Hunter Liggett, an active Army installation, and reaching it can require an ID check. Check hours and Mass times for each mission before you go -- several close for weddings and funerals with no notice.

A note on the bells: the cast-iron mission bells on their shepherd's-crook posts are a 1906 commemorative marker, not a colonial artifact. About 450 were placed originally, and a restoration program has been replacing missing ones from the original molds since 1996.
trail.go_deeper:
The California Missions Foundation (californiamissionsfoundation.org) is the best single starting point, with a page for every mission and current visiting information.

Each mission's own website carries its Mass schedule; those links are on the individual mission pages here. Several missions have museums with collections documenting the Native communities who built them, and a number of California tribal nations publish their own histories of the mission period -- worth reading alongside the mission's account of itself.
trail.notes_internal: Researched September 2026. Founding dates and founders follow the California Missions Foundation and each mission's own site; where the traditional count credits Serra but another friar celebrated the first Mass (San Gabriel, San Francisco de Asis, Santa Clara), the celebrant is named. The 600-mile figure is the modern commemorative route, not a surveyed colonial road.

sites.title: Mission San Diego de Alcalá
sites.summary_short: Mission San Diego de Alcalá is the first of California's 21 missions, founded in 1769 on the hill above San Diego Bay. Pilgrims come to pray where the Catholic faith in California began and to honor Father Luis Jayme, the state's first Christian martyr.
sites.the_story:
St. Junípero Serra raised the cross here on July 16, 1769, on Presidio Hill overlooking San Diego Bay. Water was scarce and the soil poor, so in 1774 the friars moved the mission about six miles up the San Diego River to its present site. In November 1775, Kumeyaay people who resisted the new order attacked and burned the mission. Father Luis Jayme walked out to meet them and was killed. He is remembered as California's first Christian martyr, and his remains rest beneath the sanctuary floor.

The friars rebuilt in adobe, this time fortified. Heavy buttresses added after a cracked roof in 1811 helped the church survive the great earthquake of 1812. After secularization the property passed to the U.S. Army, and President Abraham Lincoln returned it to the Catholic Church in 1862. A careful restoration in 1931 brought back the 1813 church.

Today it is an active parish of the Diocese of San Diego and, since 1976, a minor basilica. Visitors see the 46-foot bell wall with its five bronze bells, the quiet garden courtyard, the museum, the excavated foundations of the earlier churches, and La Casa de Padre Serra, whose small bedroom is the one original room to survive.
sites.church_recognition:
Mission San Diego de Alcalá was founded on July 16, 1769 by St. Junípero Serra. It is the first of the twenty-one missions of Alta California, and today it is minor basilica and active parish church. It holds the title of minor basilica.

The mission was built by Native Californians, and the Church has publicly acknowledged the coercion and harm that mission life involved. That history is told in full on the California Mission Trail page, and it belongs to this place as much as its founding date does.

sites.title: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo (Carmel Mission)
sites.summary_short: Carmel Mission was St. Junípero Serra's home and the headquarters of the whole mission chain. He is buried beneath the sanctuary, which makes this the most important pilgrimage stop on the trail for anyone following his life.
sites.the_story:
Serra founded this mission at Monterey on June 3, 1770, then moved it the following year to the mouth of the Carmel River, away from the soldiers of the presidio and closer to good water and farmland. From 1770 to 1803 Carmel served as headquarters for every mission in Alta California, and Serra directed the work of the chain from a small cell here. He died at Carmel on August 28, 1784, and was buried beneath the sanctuary floor beside his friend Juan Crespí.

Serra had asked for a stone church, and it was finished in 1797 under the master mason Manuel Ruiz. Its curved ceiling, star window, and off-center bell tower are unlike anything else in the chain. After secularization the roof fell in, and the building stood open to the sky until restoration work began in the 1880s and was completed by Harry Downie starting in 1931.

Pope John XXIII named the church a minor basilica in 1960, and Pope Francis canonized Serra in 2015. Visitors today find the stone church, Serra's reconstructed cell, the Jo Mora cenotaph, several museum rooms, California's first library, and quiet gardens.

sites.title: Mission San Antonio de Padua
sites.summary_short: Mission San Antonio de Padua sits alone in a wide valley in the Santa Lucia Mountains, with no town built up around it. It is the quietest mission on the trail and the best place to see what the setting actually looked like in the 1700s.
sites.the_story:
Serra founded San Antonio de Padua on July 14, 1771, in oak country far inland from the coast. Two years later the friars moved it a short distance to the Valley of the Oaks, where the San Antonio River gave a steadier supply of water. With the Salinan people who lived there, they built what is often called the most complete water system of the mission era, including dams, aqueducts, a reservoir, and a working grist mill.

The mission was also an early workshop for building methods that spread down the chain, including fired clay roof tiles that resisted fire far better than thatch. The friars taught music using colored notation, and one of the first recorded marriages in California took place here in 1773. After secularization the buildings fell into ruin; the Historic Landmarks League and later the Hearst Foundation funded the restoration that brought the church back.

Because the surrounding land became Fort Hunter Liggett, no city grew up around the mission. Visitors reach it by a long country road and find the restored church, a museum of mission-era tools and instruments, gardens, and a retreat house. It is still used for Mass and for group retreats.

sites.title: Mission San Gabriel Arcángel
sites.summary_short: Mission San Gabriel was the wealthiest mission in the chain and the seed from which Los Angeles grew. Its unusual Moorish-looking church reopened in 2023 after a fire, and its cemetery is the oldest in Los Angeles County.
sites.the_story:
Two Franciscans, Pedro Cambón and Ángel Somera, founded San Gabriel on September 8, 1771, on the feast of Mary's Nativity, acting under Serra as father president. In 1775 the mission moved about three miles to better farmland. It became so productive in grain, cattle, and wine that it was called the Pride of the Missions and sent supplies to the rest of the chain. The settlers who founded the pueblo of Los Angeles in 1781 set out from here.

Father Antonio Cruzado, born near Córdoba in Spain, designed the church, and its capped buttresses and long side wall echo the cathedral of his home city. It is unlike any other mission church in California. Earthquakes in 1804, 1812, and 1987 each did damage, and on July 11, 2020, an arson fire destroyed the roof and gutted the interior.

The church was rebuilt and reopened in July 2023. Visitors see the restored interior, the six-bell campanario, the old winery and kitchen buildings, a museum, and the cemetery, where roughly 6,000 people are buried, most of them Tongva. It remains an active parish of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles.

sites.title: Mission San Luis Obispo de Tolosa
sites.summary_short: Mission San Luis Obispo de Tolosa stands right in the middle of downtown San Luis Obispo, still serving as the town's Catholic parish. It is an easy, welcoming stop where the mission and the modern city share the same plaza.
sites.the_story:
Serra founded the fifth mission on September 1, 1772, in a valley the Spanish had already nicknamed La Cañada de los Osos, the Valley of the Bears, after hunting there during a famine the year before. He named it for St. Louis of Toulouse, a young Franciscan bishop. Chumash and Salinan people lived in the surrounding villages and built the mission.

Early buildings were roofed with thatch, which burned easily when fire arrows were shot onto them during periods of conflict. Tradition credits the friars here with turning to fired clay roof tiles in response, a method that spread through the chain and became one of the defining marks of mission architecture. The church has an unusual L-shaped plan, with the belfry and vestibule joined to the nave.

The mission was covered over with clapboard and a New England-style steeple in the 1800s, then stripped back to its original adobe lines in a restoration finished in 1934. Today it is an active parish of the Diocese of Monterey. Visitors find the church, a good museum of Chumash and mission material, and a plaza and creek walk just outside the doors.

sites.title: Mission San Francisco de Asís (Mission Dolores)
sites.summary_short: Mission Dolores holds the oldest intact building in San Francisco, a small adobe chapel from 1791 that came through the 1906 earthquake unharmed. Next to it stands a minor basilica, and behind both lies a cemetery where thousands of Ohlone and Miwok people are buried.
sites.the_story:
Father Francisco Palóu celebrated the first Mass at a camp near a small lagoon on June 29, 1776, five days before the Declaration of Independence was signed on the other side of the continent. The mission was formally dedicated on October 9, 1776, and named for St. Francis of Assisi, though everyone came to call it Mission Dolores after the nearby Arroyo de los Dolores.

The adobe chapel finished in 1791 is the oldest intact building in San Francisco. Its four-foot walls and redwood roof beams, lashed with rawhide, held firm through the 1906 earthquake and fire that leveled much of the city. Inside are the original redwood ceiling painted in Ohlone designs and an altar brought from Mexico.

A far larger church was built beside the chapel in 1918 and raised to the rank of minor basilica by Pope Pius XII in 1952. The cemetery between them is one of the few original burial grounds left in the city, and it holds an estimated 5,000 Ohlone and Miwok graves, most of them unmarked. A memorial and a reconstructed tule hut honor them.

sites.title: Mission San Juan Capistrano
sites.summary_short: Mission San Juan Capistrano holds the Serra Chapel, the oldest standing church in California and the only surviving church where St. Junípero Serra said Mass. The dramatic ruins of its Great Stone Church stand nearby, and the mission is famous for the swallows that return each spring.
sites.the_story:
Father Lasuén first raised the cross here on October 30, 1775, but news of the attack at San Diego forced the party to withdraw within days. Serra returned and refounded the mission on November 1, 1776, digging up the bells that had been buried for safekeeping. The Acjachemen people of the surrounding villages built and worked the mission, which became the first place in California to smelt iron from ore.

The adobe Serra Chapel was finished in 1782 and is the oldest standing church in California. It is the only surviving church in the state where Serra himself celebrated Mass and baptized. Its gilded Baroque altarpiece was brought from Barcelona in 1906, and a side chapel honors St. Peregrine, patron of those with cancer.

The Great Stone Church, begun in 1797 and finished in 1806, was the most ambitious building in the chain. On December 8, 1812, an earthquake brought down its vaults and tower during morning Mass, killing about forty worshippers. Its ruins still stand. Four of its bells now hang in a bell wall. Visitors also see the gardens, the old soldiers' barracks, and the swallows that return each spring.
sites.church_recognition:

It is the seventh of the twenty-one missions of Alta California, and today it is historic mission and museum, with the serra chapel still used for mass.

The mission was built by Native Californians, and the Church has publicly acknowledged the coercion and harm that mission life involved. That history is told in full on the California Mission Trail page, and it belongs to this place as much as its founding date does.

sites.title: Mission Santa Clara de Asís
sites.summary_short: Mission Santa Clara is the only mission that stands on a university campus, serving as the chapel of Santa Clara University. It was the first California mission named for a woman saint, and it is still used daily for Mass.
sites.the_story:
Fray Tomás de la Peña celebrated the first Mass beside the Guadalupe River on January 12, 1777, founding the eighth mission under Serra's direction. It was the first in California named for a woman, St. Clare of Assisi, the founder of the Poor Clares and companion of St. Francis. The Ohlone people of the Santa Clara Valley built and sustained it.

No mission moved more often. Floods, earthquakes, and fire pushed the community to six different church buildings over 150 years. Serra blessed the site of the third church in 1781. An earthquake wrecked the church in 1818, and a fire destroyed its successor in 1926. The church standing today was dedicated in 1928 and was designed to recall the 1825 building, with painted decoration reproduced from the old ceiling.

After secularization the property passed to the Jesuits, who founded Santa Clara University here in 1851, making it the oldest college in California and the only one in the state descended from a Spanish mission. The bell tower holds bells cast in the late 1700s along with one sent by King Alfonso XIII of Spain in 1929. Adobe walls, an old lodge, and the Mission Gardens survive from the earlier missions.

sites.title: Mission San Buenaventura
sites.summary_short: Mission San Buenaventura was the last mission St. Junípero Serra founded himself, and it sits in the heart of downtown Ventura. Pope Francis raised it to a minor basilica in 2020, and it is still a busy parish church.
sites.the_story:
Serra founded San Buenaventura on Easter Sunday, March 31, 1782, nine years after he first planned it. It was the ninth mission and the last he founded in person; he died two years later. He named it for St. Bonaventure, the great Franciscan theologian. The Chumash people of the coastal villages built the mission and its remarkable seven-mile aqueduct, which carried water from the Ventura River to gardens famous enough that visiting sailors wrote home about the fruit.

The stone and adobe church standing today was completed in 1809 and repaired after the 1812 earthquake. It keeps a set of wooden bells found nowhere else in the chain, thought to have been used during Holy Week. Restoration in 1957 removed Victorian-era alterations and returned the interior to something close to its mission-era look.

On June 9, 2020, Pope Francis raised the church to the rank of minor basilica, the fourth mission church to hold that title. It remains an active parish of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles serving about 2,000 families. Visitors find the church, a small museum with Chumash baskets and mission-era objects, a garden courtyard, and the old olive press.

sites.title: Mission Santa Bárbara
sites.summary_short: Known as the Queen of the Missions for its twin bell towers and hillside setting, Mission Santa Bárbara is the only mission that Franciscan friars have served without a break since it was founded. It is a parish, a museum, a friary, and a research archive all at once.
sites.the_story:
Father Fermín Francisco de Lasuén founded Santa Bárbara on December 4, 1786, the feast of St. Barbara, two years after Serra's death. Serra had hoped to found it himself but was blocked by a dispute with the governor. The Chumash people, who lived in large coastal towns along this stretch of the channel, built the mission and its stone waterworks, including a reservoir still used by the city and a lavandería fed through a carved stone spout.

The 1812 earthquake destroyed the third church, and the stone church that replaced it was finished in 1820. Its façade was drawn from a Roman treatise on architecture, and a matching second tower was added in 1831, giving the mission the twin-towered front that earned it the name Queen of the Missions. The 1925 earthquake brought the towers down, and they were rebuilt.

Santa Bárbara later became the headquarters of the mission chain and the seat of California's first bishop in 1842. Franciscans have served here continuously since 1786, one of only two missions where that is true. Visitors see the church and its six bells, the cemetery and Chumash burial ground, the museum rooms, the gardens, and the Mission Archive-Library, which holds documents dating back to the 1760s.

sites.title: Mission La Purísima Concepción
sites.summary_short: La Purísima is the most completely restored mission in California, with its church, shops, quarters, and workshops all rebuilt and furnished. It is the best place on the trail to understand how a mission actually worked day to day.
sites.the_story:
Lasuén founded La Purísima Concepción on December 8, 1787, the feast of the Immaculate Conception, near what is now the city of Lompoc. The Chumash people of the surrounding villages built it. The great earthquake of December 21, 1812, and the rains that followed destroyed the mission, and the community rebuilt about four miles northeast in a new location.

The rebuilt mission was laid out in an unusual straight line rather than the usual enclosed quadrangle, possibly so people could get out quickly in another earthquake. It prospered until an 1824 Chumash uprising, which began at Santa Inés and ended here after a month-long occupation and a negotiated surrender. After secularization the buildings melted back into the ground.

Between 1934 and 1942 the Civilian Conservation Corps rebuilt the mission using original methods, making adobe bricks and roof tiles by hand on site. The result is the only place in California where a complete Spanish mission complex can be walked through. It is now a state historic park with the church, friars' quarters, workshops, blacksmith shop, water system, gardens, and livestock. It is a park rather than a parish, though Mass is celebrated there on special occasions.

sites.title: Mission Santa Cruz
sites.summary_short: Mission Santa Cruz is the smallest stop on the trail, a half-size replica chapel built in 1931 after the original church collapsed in an earthquake. A block away, an adobe from 1824 preserves rooms where Native families lived.
sites.the_story:
Lasuén founded the twelfth mission on August 28, 1791, and named it for the Holy Cross. It had a hard history. In 1797 the Spanish planted a pueblo of retired soldiers and former convicts directly across the river, and those neighbors took mission crops and labor for years. When the privateer Hipólito Bouchard threatened the coast in 1818, the community evacuated and townspeople looted what was left behind.

Secularization in 1834 finished the decline, and earthquakes in 1857 brought down the church tower and walls. Nothing of the original church remains standing. In 1931 a replica chapel was built nearby at roughly a third the size of the original, paid for by a local benefactor. It holds statues, paintings, and a chalice associated with the mission era.

The active parish next door, Holy Cross Church, dates from 1889 and serves the neighborhood today. A block downhill, the Santa Cruz Mission State Historic Park preserves the 1824 Neary-Rodriguez Adobe, a surviving section of the mission's long adobe row that housed Native families, and it is one of the very few such buildings left anywhere in California. Visitors can see both in an easy walk.

sites.title: Mission Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
sites.summary_short: Mission Soledad is the loneliest and least visited mission on the trail, set among farm fields in the Salinas Valley. Its name means Our Lady of Solitude, and the small rebuilt chapel and the ruins around it suit that title.
sites.the_story:
Lasuén founded Nuestra Señora de la Soledad on October 9, 1791, in a windy stretch of the Salinas Valley. The name came from a misunderstanding years earlier, when a Native woman answered the Portolá expedition with a word the Spanish heard as soledad, solitude. The Esselen and Ohlone people of the valley built and worked the mission.

Life here was harder than at most missions. Floods repeatedly destroyed the church, crops failed, and epidemics struck the community. Governor José Joaquín de Arrillaga died at Soledad in 1814 and is buried in the chapel. Father Vicente Francisco de Sarría, who had served the mission for years, collapsed and died at the altar in 1835, by then the last friar left, ministering to the few who remained.

After secularization the adobe walls dissolved in the rains. The Native Daughters of the Golden West rebuilt the small chapel in 1955, and the wing beside it was restored in the 1960s as a museum. Visitors today find the chapel, the museum rooms, a cemetery, a garden, and low melted adobe ruins that outline the old quadrangle. It is a quiet stop and easy to reach from Highway 101.

sites.title: Mission San José
sites.summary_short: Mission San José was one of the largest and most productive missions, famous in its day for a thirty-piece Native orchestra. The adobe church visitors see today is a careful reconstruction of the 1809 original, completed in 1985.
sites.the_story:
Lasuén founded Mission San José on June 11, 1797, at the foot of the East Bay hills. Under Father Narciso Durán, who served here for 27 years, it became one of the richest missions in the chain, second only to San Luis Rey in size. Durán taught music to the Ohlone and Yokuts people of the community and built a thirty-piece orchestra whose reputation carried up and down California.

The mission also stood at a hard frontier. In 1828 Estanislao, a Yokuts man raised at the mission, led hundreds of people in a revolt in the Central Valley that took several military expeditions to put down. His name survives in the Stanislaus River and county.

The 1868 Hayward earthquake destroyed the adobe church. A wooden Gothic-style parish church stood on the site for over a century, and in 1982 it was moved to Burlingame so the mission church could be rebuilt. Using original methods and surviving plans, the 1809 church was reconstructed and dedicated in 1985. The surviving monastery wing next door, the only original mission building left, now houses the museum. It is an active parish of the Diocese of Oakland.

sites.title: Mission San Juan Bautista
sites.summary_short: Mission San Juan Bautista has the largest church of the 21 missions, the only one with three aisles, and Mass has been said here without a break since 1797. It faces a Spanish plaza that still looks much as it did in the 1800s.
sites.the_story:
Lasuén founded San Juan Bautista on June 24, 1797, the feast of St. John the Baptist. The Mutsun Ohlone people of the surrounding villages built the mission. The church was designed unusually wide, with three aisles divided by arches, to hold a growing community, and it is the largest of the mission churches.

The 1812 earthquake damaged the arches badly, and the friars walled up the side aisles for safety. They stayed closed for more than 160 years until a 1975 restoration reopened them and restored the original three-aisle plan. The floor tiles still carry the paw prints of animals that walked across them while they dried in the sun two centuries ago. The church holds the most complete set of apostolate paintings in the chain.

The mission sits directly on the San Andreas Fault, and an exhibit outside the walls marks the fault line and a surviving stretch of El Camino Real. The plaza in front is preserved as San Juan Bautista State Historic Park, with the Plaza Hotel, stable, and other 1800s buildings around it, so a visitor sees not only a mission but a whole Spanish-era town.

sites.title: Mission San Miguel Arcángel
sites.summary_short: Mission San Miguel has the only mission interior in California whose original wall paintings have never been repainted or touched up. Walking in is the closest a visitor can come to seeing a mission church exactly as the people who built it left it.
sites.the_story:
Lasuén founded San Miguel Arcángel on July 25, 1797, in the Salinas River valley, filling the long gap between San Antonio and San Luis Obispo. The Salinan people of the region built it. A fire in 1806 destroyed the first church and most of the year's harvest.

The replacement church, finished in 1818, has adobe walls six feet thick. Its interior was painted by Salinan artists working with the Catalan craftsman Esteban Munras, and those frescoes, including a painted all-seeing eye above the altar and columns and cornices done in trompe l'oeil, have never been retouched or repainted. No other mission can say that.

Secularization stripped the mission, and for decades parts of it served as a saloon, a store, and a dance hall. The Franciscans returned in 1928. The 2003 San Simeon earthquake caused serious damage and closed the church for six years; it reopened in 2009 after a major seismic retrofit, and the National Trust for Historic Preservation had listed it among America's most endangered places. Today it is an active parish of the Diocese of Monterey, with a museum, a long arched corridor, a cemetery holding about 2,000 burials, and gardens.

sites.title: Mission San Fernando Rey de España
sites.summary_short: Mission San Fernando is best known for its Convento, a long two-story adobe with nineteen arches that is the largest freestanding adobe building in California. The mission gave the San Fernando Valley its name.
sites.the_story:
Lasuén founded San Fernando Rey de España on September 8, 1797, closing the gap between San Buenaventura on the coast and San Gabriel inland. It was named for St. Ferdinand III, the 13th-century king of Castile. The Tataviam, Tongva, and Chumash people of the valley built it, and the valley took its name from the mission.

Because it sat on the main road to Los Angeles, San Fernando took in a steady stream of travelers, and the friars built the Convento to house them. Finished in 1822 after twelve years of work, it runs more than 240 feet with a colonnade of nineteen arches and holds over twenty rooms on two floors. It is the largest freestanding adobe structure in California and the mission's signature sight.

The church was damaged repeatedly by earthquakes, most severely in the 1971 Sylmar quake, and was rebuilt as an exact replica in 1974. Today the mission serves as a chapel of ease of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles rather than a full parish, and the grounds operate as a museum. Visitors see the church with its painted decoration and carved statue of St. Ferdinand sent by the king of Spain, the Convento, a Córdoba-style fountain, a replica winery, gardens, and a memorial garden.

sites.title: Mission San Luis Rey de Francia
sites.summary_short: Called the King of the Missions, San Luis Rey was the largest and most prosperous of the 21 and is still the biggest mission complex in California. Franciscans have served here almost continuously, and it now runs a busy retreat center alongside the parish.
sites.the_story:
Lasuén founded San Luis Rey de Francia on June 13, 1798, naming it for the 13th-century French king St. Louis IX. The Payómkawichum, known to the Spanish as the Luiseño, built and worked the mission. Under Father Antonio Peyri, who stayed 34 years, it grew faster than any other: by 1825 nearly 2,900 people lived in the community, more than triple the usual mission population, and its lands ran fifteen miles out in every direction with over 50,000 head of livestock.

The church finished in 1815 is cruciform, the only mission church built on that plan, and it is crowned by a wooden dome and lantern that light the crossing. Below the mission a sunken garden holds the tiled lavandería where the community washed and where California's first pepper tree, planted in 1830, still grows.

After secularization the buildings were abandoned and the U.S. Army used them; Franciscans returned in 1892. Today San Luis Rey is a parish of the Diocese of San Diego, a Franciscan community, a museum, and a retreat center. Visitors see the church, the museum, the cemetery, the gardens, and a complex that still covers about six acres.

sites.title: Mission Santa Inés
sites.summary_short: Mission Santa Inés sits on a bluff above the Santa Ynez Valley at the edge of Solvang, with long views over the hills. It is an active parish and holds one of the finest collections of mission-era vestments in California.
sites.the_story:
Father Estévan Tapís, who had succeeded Lasuén as father president, founded Santa Inés on September 17, 1804. It was built to serve Chumash people living inland from Santa Bárbara and La Purísima who had a hard journey over the mountains to reach a mission. It is named for St. Agnes of Rome, the young Roman martyr.

The 1812 earthquake destroyed much of the mission, and the church that replaced it was finished in 1817. In February 1824 a soldier's flogging of a Chumash man here set off the largest Native uprising of the mission era, which spread to La Purísima and Santa Bárbara before it was settled. In 1844 the mission became the site of California's first seminary, the College of Our Lady of Refuge.

The buildings decayed badly after secularization, and long restorations in the 20th century, including work after a 1911 collapse of the bell wall, brought back the church and the arcade. Today it is an active parish of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles. Visitors see the church with its painted reredos, the bell wall, the arched colonnade, the gardens and cemetery, and a museum whose vestment collection is among the best in the chain.

sites.title: Mission San Rafael Arcángel
sites.summary_short: Mission San Rafael began not as a mission but as a hospital, a warmer place to send people who were falling sick at foggy Mission Dolores. Nothing original survives, but a 1949 replica chapel stands beside the modern parish church on the original site.
sites.the_story:
San Rafael Arcángel was founded on December 14, 1817, as an asistencia, a branch hospital for Mission Dolores across the bay. San Francisco's cold and fog were killing people in large numbers, and the friars looked for a sheltered, sunny spot in Marin. They named it for St. Raphael the Archangel, whose name means God heals. Father Vicente Francisco de Sarría led the founding, assisted by Frs. Narciso Durán, Ramón Abella, and Luis Gil y Taboada, who had some medical training.

The experiment worked well enough that in 1822 San Rafael was raised to a full mission. Coast Miwok people made up most of the community. The mission was secularized in 1834, and its buildings were sold, torn down, and quarried for materials; by 1870 nothing of the original was left, and a parish church went up on the site.

In 1949, using a sketch made by a traveler in the 1820s, a replica of the mission chapel was built next to the modern St. Raphael church. It is small and plain, with a star window over the door and three bells hung outside. Visitors see the replica chapel, a small gift shop and museum, and the parish grounds in downtown San Rafael.

sites.title: Mission San Francisco Solano
sites.summary_short: Mission San Francisco Solano in Sonoma is the last and northernmost of the 21 missions, and the only one founded after Mexico won independence from Spain. It marks the end of the mission trail and is preserved today as a museum.
sites.the_story:
Father José Altimira, a young friar unhappy at Mission Dolores, raised the cross at Sonoma on July 4, 1823, with the backing of the Mexican governor but without the approval of his own church superiors. His plan was to close Dolores and San Rafael and move everyone north. The bishop's representatives overruled that, but they let the new mission stand. It is the only one of the 21 founded under Mexican rule rather than Spanish, and the only one founded without church permission first.

Altimira's harshness drove the Coast Miwok, Pomo, Wappo, and Patwin people of the community to revolt in 1826, and he fled. Under Father Buenaventura Fortuni the mission stabilized, and the adobe chapel standing today was built in 1841 by General Mariano Vallejo after secularization. Above its altar is the Eye of Heaven, an opening that lets light fall on the sanctuary.

Sonoma's plaza just outside became the site of the Bear Flag Revolt on June 14, 1846, when settlers declared California a republic. The mission was damaged in the 1906 earthquake and later restored. It is now California Historical Landmark No. 1 in the state's numbering of the missions and part of Sonoma State Historic Park, operating as a museum rather than a parish.
